title: Is Gatorade Good for a Hangover? What It Fixes and What It Doesn't
excerpt: Does Gatorade help a hangover? What it can and can't fix, which version works best (Gatorlyte, Zero, regular), how it compares to water and Pedialyte, and how to drink it.
metaDescription: Is Gatorade good for a hangover? What it fixes, what it doesn't, the best version (Gatorlyte, Zero, regular), and how it compares to water and Pedialyte.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Gatorade is a reasonable hangover drink, but it only fixes part of the problem. It puts water and a bit of sodium back in your body, and its sugar can help with the weak, shaky, low-energy feeling. That can ease thirst, dry mouth, and some of the headache. It won't do much for nausea, fatigue, or brain fog, because those come mostly from how your body breaks down alcohol, not from being dried out. So yes, drink it if you like it. Just don't expect a bottle of Gatorade to undo a rough night.

**The quick rules:** Sip, don't chug. Pair it with food that has some salt in it. If you want a stronger rehydration drink, pick **Gatorlyte** over regular Gatorade. If you want to skip the sugar, **Gatorade Zero** keeps the electrolytes. And if plain water is what you have, water plus a salty snack does most of the same job for free.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and product labels in plain language. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, you've been vomiting repeatedly, or you have signs of serious dehydration: dizziness or fainting when you stand, confusion, a racing heart that won't settle, very dark urine, or barely urinating at all. Check with your doctor before using electrolyte drinks regularly if you have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure, or have been told to limit sodium, and keep an eye on sugar if you have diabetes. If someone after a night of drinking can't be woken, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, has seizures, or has blue-tinged or very pale, cold skin, **call 911**. That's possible alcohol poisoning, and no drink fixes it.

## Does Gatorade Help a Hangover? What It Can and Can't Do

To see where Gatorade fits, it helps to know what a hangover actually is. It isn't one problem. It's a cluster of things happening at once:

- **Dehydration.** Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink, so you wake up short on fluid.
- **Your body processing the alcohol.** As your liver breaks alcohol down, it makes a toxic in-between chemical called acetaldehyde. Researchers also point to an immune response, a kind of low-level inflammation, as a big driver of how bad you feel.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night, so you wake up unrested.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and slows digestion, which feeds the nausea.
- **Low blood sugar in some people.** Alcohol can interfere with how your liver releases sugar into your blood, which may add to shakiness and weakness.

Gatorade speaks to the first item directly and touches the last one a little. That's it. A widely cited review of hangover research in the *Annals of Internal Medicine* (Wiese and colleagues, 2000) noted that dehydration and electrolyte changes don't line up neatly with how severe a hangover feels. Later reviews from hangover researchers have made the same point: being dehydrated and being hungover often happen together, but they aren't the same thing, and fixing one doesn't fix the other.

Here's a realistic picture of what to expect:

| Hangover symptom | Can Gatorade help? |
|---|---|
| Thirst and dry mouth | Yes. This is what it's good at. |
| Headache | Partly. Some hangover headache comes from fluid loss, some doesn't. |
| Dizziness when standing | Partly, if it's from low fluid. |
| Weak, shaky, low-energy feeling | A little, from the sugar. |
| Nausea | Sometimes, if sipped slowly. Gulping can make it worse. |
| Fatigue and brain fog | Not really. These come mostly from poor sleep and alcohol processing. |
| Anxiety and low mood | No. |

So the useful way to think about Gatorade is as a rehydration tool, not a hangover cure. If dehydration is your main complaint, it can make a real difference. If you mostly feel poisoned and exhausted, it won't.

## Why Alcohol Dries You Out in the First Place

Your brain normally releases a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Alcohol suppresses that hormone. With the brake off, your kidneys send more water to your bladder than they otherwise would. That's why you end up making trip after trip to the bathroom once you start drinking.

On top of that, a night out often means sweating in a warm room, dancing, maybe vomiting, and not drinking much plain water. Then you sleep for several hours without drinking anything. By morning you're short on water, and you've lost some sodium and potassium along the way.

That's the gap Gatorade was designed to fill, though it was designed to fill it for athletes losing fluid through sweat, not for people recovering from a night of drinking. The difference matters, and it shows up in the label.

## What's Actually in Gatorade (and Each Version Compared)

Gatorade makes several versions, and they're not interchangeable for a hangover. Here are approximate numbers per 20-ounce bottle for the main ones. Exact amounts vary by flavor and format and change over time, so check the label on the one you buy.

| Per 20 fl oz (approx.) | Sodium | Potassium | Sugar | Calories |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gatorade Thirst Quencher (regular) | ~270 mg | ~75 mg | ~34 g | ~140 |
| Gatorade Zero | ~270 mg | ~75 mg | 0 g | ~10 |
| G2 (lower sugar) | ~270 mg | ~75 mg | ~12 g | ~50 |
| Gatorlyte | ~490 mg | ~350 mg | ~12 g | ~50 |
| Powerade (for comparison) | ~250 mg | ~80 mg | ~34 g | ~130 |

A few things stand out:

- **Regular Gatorade is mostly sugar water with a pinch of salt.** About 34 grams of sugar is close to what's in a 12-ounce can of soda. The sodium is real but modest.
- **Gatorade Zero and G2 keep the same electrolytes with less or no sugar.** They're sweetened with low- or no-calorie sweeteners instead.
- **Gatorlyte is the outlier.** It has nearly twice the sodium and several times the potassium of regular Gatorade, with about a third of the sugar. It was built as a "rapid rehydration" drink, and it's the closest thing in the Gatorade lineup to a medical rehydration solution.
- **Powerade is basically the same idea as regular Gatorade.** If you're standing in a store choosing between the two for a hangover, pick whichever you like the taste of. The difference is small.

### How that compares to a real rehydration solution

Medical rehydration drinks are built around a specific ratio of salt to sugar. The World Health Organization's oral rehydration solution, used worldwide to treat dehydration from diarrhea, has much more sodium than a sports drink and much less sugar. A regular sports drink has roughly a quarter to a third of the sodium concentration of that formula, and noticeably more sugar.

That matters because of how your gut absorbs fluid. Your intestine pulls in sodium and glucose together, and water follows them. A small amount of sugar actually helps. Too much sugar relative to salt doesn't add much benefit, and for some people a very sweet drink sits badly on an already queasy stomach.

A 2016 study in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* (Maughan and colleagues) compared how well different drinks kept people hydrated over several hours. An oral rehydration solution and milk came out ahead of water. A regular sports drink performed about the same as plain water. That's not a knock on Gatorade, but it's a useful reality check: regular Gatorade is closer to water with flavor than to a medical rehydration drink.

## Which Gatorade Is Best for a Hangover?

If you're going to drink Gatorade the morning after, here's how to pick:

**Best overall: Gatorlyte.** More sodium, more potassium, less sugar. If dehydration is your main complaint, this is the one that actually behaves like a rehydration drink. It also tends to cost more than regular Gatorade.

**Best if you want no sugar: Gatorade Zero.** Same electrolytes as the regular version without the sugar. A good choice if you're watching sugar or calories, or if sweet drinks turn your stomach. The one trade-off is that you lose the carbs, which help your gut take in sodium and can lift the shaky feeling. If you're eating something alongside it, that hardly matters.

**Fine if it's what you have: regular Gatorade or Powerade.** It still helps you rehydrate, and the sugar can help if you feel weak or haven't eaten. Just don't drink three bottles of it, because that's over 100 grams of sugar.

**Middle ground: G2.** Less sugar than regular, a little more than Zero. Fine for the job, nothing special.

### Does the color matter?

No. People online swear by a particular flavor, often a blue, red, or lemon-lime one, but there's no difference in what they do. The electrolytes and sugar are essentially the same across flavors within a product line. Pick the one you can stand to drink when you feel awful. That's the one that will actually get finished.

## Gatorade vs Water vs Pedialyte for a Hangover

These are the three drinks most people reach for. Here's the honest comparison.

**Water** handles the core problem, which is being short on fluid. It's free, it has no sugar, and for a mild hangover it's usually enough, especially if you eat something salty with it. Its weakness is that it has no sodium, so on its own it's absorbed and held a bit less efficiently than a drink with electrolytes, and if you drink a lot of it quickly you'll mostly just pee it out.

**Gatorade** adds modest sodium and a good amount of sugar. That gives it a small edge over water for holding fluid and for the low-energy feeling, and many people find it easier to drink when they're queasy. The downside is the sugar load in the regular version.

**Pedialyte** was designed as a medical rehydration drink. It has roughly twice the sodium and several times the potassium of regular Gatorade, with less than half the sugar. On paper it's the stronger choice for rehydration. It also costs more. We compare the two head to head, with numbers and cost per serving, in our [Pedialyte vs Gatorade hangover guide](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover). For a wider lineup that includes LMNT, Liquid I.V., and other electrolyte mixes, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangover comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

| | Water | Regular Gatorade | Gatorlyte | Pedialyte |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rehydration | Good | Good | Better | Better |
| Sodium | None | Modest | High | High |
| Sugar | None | High | Low | Low |
| Easy on a queasy stomach | Usually | Often, if sipped | Often | Often |
| Cost | Free | Low | Moderate | Higher |

The practical takeaway: for a mild hangover, any of these plus some food will do. If you're properly dried out, maybe after a lot of drinking, a hot day, or some vomiting, a higher-sodium option like Gatorlyte or Pedialyte is worth the extra money. If you want other options, including coconut water, broth, and milk, our guide to the [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) ranks them, and our [coconut water for hangovers](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) page covers that one in detail.

## How to Drink Gatorade for a Hangover

How you drink it matters almost as much as what you drink.

1. **Start with a glass of water or a small Gatorade before bed.** Not a full liter. Enough to take the edge off. Drinking a huge amount at bedtime mostly means waking up to use the bathroom, which cuts into sleep you need.
2. **In the morning, sip.** Aim for small, steady sips over 20 to 30 minutes rather than downing a bottle in one go. A stomach irritated by alcohol handles small amounts better, and your body absorbs fluid better when it arrives gradually.
3. **Eat something.** Toast, eggs, a banana, soup, or anything with a bit of salt. Food helps your blood sugar, gives your gut something to work with, and adds sodium and potassium that a regular sports drink is light on. If eggs sound good, our [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) page explains why they're a solid choice.
4. **Alternate with water.** One bottle of regular Gatorade is plenty of sugar. After that, switch to water or a low-sugar option.
5. **Watch your urine.** Pale yellow means you're doing fine. Dark yellow means keep going. Clear and frequent means you can ease off.

### If you're nauseous

Nausea is where people often go wrong with Gatorade. Gulping a cold, sweet drink on an upset stomach can bring it straight back up. Instead:

- Take a few small sips, wait five minutes, then take a few more.
- Try it cold, or over ice. Many people find cold drinks easier to keep down.
- If regular Gatorade feels too sweet, try diluting it half and half with water, or switch to Gatorade Zero.
- Pair it with something bland, like crackers or dry toast, once you can.

If you're still vomiting after several hours, or you can't keep any fluids down for most of the day, that's no longer a normal hangover. See a doctor or go to urgent care. Persistent vomiting can dehydrate you quickly, and you may need fluids given another way. For more on settling your stomach, see our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025).

## Should You Drink Gatorade Before or While Drinking?

A lot of people ask whether drinking Gatorade before a night out, or using it as a mixer, will head off the hangover.

**Before drinking:** being well hydrated going in is sensible, and so is eating a real meal. But there is no good evidence that a sports drink beforehand prevents a hangover. You'll still lose fluid once you start drinking, and none of the alcohol-processing part of a hangover is touched by it.

**During the night:** alternating each alcoholic drink with a glass of water or a non-alcoholic drink is one of the most practical habits you can build, mostly because it slows you down and means you drink less alcohol overall. Gatorade works for that, though water does too.

**As a mixer:** mixing alcohol with Gatorade doesn't prevent a hangover and doesn't slow how fast the alcohol hits you. Sweet mixers can also make it easier to drink more than you planned. If you like the taste, that's fine, but don't count it as protection.

We cover the timing question for electrolytes in more depth in our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).

## Common Gatorade Hangover Myths

**"Gatorade cures a hangover."** No drink cures a hangover. Gatorade helps with the dehydration part. The rest of the hangover runs its course, usually within a day.

**"The more electrolytes, the better."** Not past a point. Most healthy people after a night out are mildly short on fluid, not dangerously low on electrolytes. Chugging several high-sodium drinks back to back isn't more effective, and people with kidney, heart, or blood pressure conditions should be careful with large amounts of sodium.

**"Gatorade is better than water."** Only slightly, and only in some ways. Regular Gatorade keeps you hydrated about as well as water, with added sugar. Its main advantage is that people find it easier to drink, and the sugar can help with low energy.

**"Blue Gatorade works best."** There's no evidence that any flavor or color works better than another.

**"Gatorade Zero doesn't work because it has no sugar."** It still rehydrates you and still has the same electrolytes. You just lose the small benefit that sugar gives for absorption and energy, which food can make up for.

## When a Hangover Is More Than a Hangover

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless, and they clear within a day. A few situations are different, and Gatorade isn't the answer to them.

**See a doctor or go to urgent care if:**

- You can't keep fluids down for most of a day, or you keep vomiting
- You feel faint or dizzy every time you stand up, or you've fainted
- Your heart is racing or pounding and doesn't settle with rest
- You're barely urinating, or your urine is very dark for many hours despite drinking
- The "hangover" is still bad after more than a day, or is getting worse instead of better
- You have kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes and you're unwell after drinking

**Call 911 right away if someone who has been drinking:**

- Can't be woken up, or is very hard to wake
- Is breathing very slowly or irregularly
- Has a seizure
- Has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin
- Is vomiting while barely conscious

These are signs of possible alcohol poisoning. Don't leave the person to sleep it off, and don't try to treat it with fluids at home. Turn them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and get emergency help.

Separately, if you notice shaking hands, sweating, a racing heart, or strong anxiety in the morning after drinking heavily for several days in a row, that can be more than a hangover. It's worth mentioning to a doctor, because stopping suddenly after a long stretch of heavy drinking can sometimes need medical support. For the everyday version of morning shakiness after a big night, see our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes).

## Going After the Cause, Not Just the Dehydration

Gatorade treats the part of a hangover that's easiest to treat. If you find yourself reaching for a sports drink after most nights out, the bigger lever is what happens before and during the night: drinking less, drinking slower, eating a proper meal, and alternating with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence behind them.

Some people also add a supplement aimed at the alcohol-processing side of a hangover, which no electrolyte drink touches. The one we cover most on this site is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Here's an honest summary of where it stands: most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, and the human evidence is still limited. It's promising, not proven, and it won't replace water, food, or drinking less. If you want to try it alongside sensible hydration, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Gatorade helps with the dehydration part of a hangover: thirst, dry mouth, some of the headache, and a bit of the low-energy feeling.
- It does little for nausea, fatigue, brain fog, or anxiety, which come mostly from alcohol processing and poor sleep.
- Regular Gatorade rehydrates about as well as water, with a lot of sugar. Gatorlyte is the strongest rehydration option in the lineup. Gatorade Zero keeps the electrolytes without the sugar.
- Sip it slowly, eat something salty with it, and switch to water after a bottle.
- Color and flavor don't matter.
- If you can't keep fluids down, feel faint, or someone can't be woken after drinking, get medical help instead of reaching for another drink.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Gatorade good for a hangover?**

It helps a little. Gatorade replaces water and some sodium, and its sugar can take the edge off the shaky, low-energy feeling. That can ease thirst, dry mouth, and part of a hangover headache. It does not fix nausea, fatigue, or brain fog, which come mostly from how your body processes alcohol rather than from dehydration. Think of it as a decent way to rehydrate, not a cure.

**Is Gatorade or water better for a hangover?**

For a mild hangover they do roughly the same job, and water is free. Gatorade's small edge is its sodium and sugar, which help your body hold onto fluid and lift low energy. Research comparing drinks found regular sports drinks kept people about as hydrated as plain water, while oral rehydration solutions and milk did better. If you'd rather drink water, add a salty snack and you get most of Gatorade's benefit.

**Which Gatorade is best for a hangover?**

Gatorlyte is the best fit, because it has far more sodium and potassium than regular Gatorade and less sugar, which puts it closer to a medical rehydration drink. Gatorade Zero is a good pick if you want electrolytes without sugar. Regular Gatorade Thirst Quencher works fine too, especially if you also feel weak or shaky and want some quick carbs. The color or flavor makes no difference.

**Is Gatorade Zero good for a hangover?**

It's fine for rehydration. Gatorade Zero has about the same sodium and potassium as regular Gatorade with almost no sugar or calories. The trade-off is that you lose the carbs, which help your gut absorb sodium and can ease the low-energy feeling some people get after drinking. If you're eating breakfast alongside it, that matters less.

**Is Pedialyte better than Gatorade for a hangover?**

On paper, yes. Pedialyte has roughly twice the sodium, several times the potassium, and less than half the sugar of regular Gatorade, because it was designed as a medical rehydration drink. Gatorlyte narrows that gap. For a mild hangover the practical difference is small, and either one helps only with the dehydration part of a hangover.

**Is Gatorade good for hangover nausea?**

It can help if you sip it slowly. Small sips of a cold, lightly sweet drink are often easier to keep down than plain water, and the sugar may settle a queasy stomach a little. Gulping a full bottle tends to make nausea worse. If you can't keep any fluids down for most of a day, or you're vomiting repeatedly, see a doctor, because you can get seriously dehydrated.

**Should I drink Gatorade before bed after drinking?**

A glass of water or Gatorade before bed is a reasonable habit, and it can help with morning thirst and dry mouth. Don't force down a huge amount, since it will mostly wake you up to use the bathroom. There is no good evidence that a pre-bed sports drink prevents a hangover. It addresses the dehydration part only.

**Can you mix Gatorade with alcohol?**

You can, but it isn't a hangover strategy. Mixing alcohol with a sports drink doesn't slow absorption or prevent a hangover, and sweet mixers can make it easier to drink more than you planned. The better approach is alternating alcoholic drinks with water or a non-alcoholic drink, and eating before and during the night.
